When I started learning Indian Sign Language with Chaitanya, who is Deaf and sits next to me in art, I thought signs were like gestures. Roughly right was good enough.
Then one lunch I signed a sentence with my palm facing out instead of facing me. Chaitanya's face went blank, then he laughed and shook his head. He showed me both versions, side by side. Same hand shape. Different direction. Completely different meaning.
"Like a vowel," he wrote on my notebook. "Bat. Bit. Not the same word."
That changed how I saw it. I'd been treating his language like loose waving. It has rules as exact as English spelling.
Now I practise with a mirror, checking where my palm points. I still get it wrong. But when I do, I ask Chaitanya to show me again, and he does.
- Elizabeth

Teacher's note - Gurleen, Sign language club, Wednesday
Damini is one of our most enthusiastic hearing learners. She has a large vocabulary for three months. But today, during the story round, the Deaf students kept looking puzzled at her.
When I watched closely, the problem was her palms. She'd get the hand shape right but let her hand face any direction. In this language, direction can change the word itself.
I asked her to sign two signs that differ only in where the palm faces. She did them the same way. When I showed her the difference, she looked surprised, then a bit embarrassed.
I told her it is like pronouncing a vowel wrongly in English, not a small detail.
She spent the rest of the session practising slowly with a partner, checking her palm every time. She said, "I thought I was being lazy. Actually I didn't know it mattered."

Sign practice at the community centre with Keerthana today. She's Deaf and is the most patient teacher on earth.

Two of our Deaf students, Rehaan and Tsering, were planning their mural in sign. Sahil, a hearing student learning to sign, sat with them.
I noticed Sahil watching their faces as much as their hands. When Tsering signed with raised eyebrows, Sahil tilted his head, then signed, "Question?" She nodded.

Sunday
Uday's family came for lunch. Uday is my cousin and he's Deaf. I'd been learning signs from videos for a month, so I was excited to show off.
First problem: half my signs were from a video made in another country. Uday laughed and showed me the ones his school uses. Some were totally different! I thought there was just one sign language. There isn't.
Second problem: when he signed fast about his cricket match, I got lost after the first bit. I nodded anyway. Then he asked me something and I had no idea what.
So I stopped pretending. I signed "Sorry, again, slow," the way Mausi taught me. Uday repeated it slower and made the ball's path in the air with his hand, and his face showed how close the match was.
This time I got it. He'd won by one run!
- Deepak

qa.a: Uday was probably pleased and relieved, because it showed Deepak really wanted to follow his story.

At the Pola festival in their village near Wardha, Lavanya stood with her friends from the district school for Deaf students, signing fast and laughing about the decorated bullocks.
Some aunties by the temple wall watched and whispered. One said loudly to Lavanya's mother, "Poor thing. If only she could talk properly."
Lavanya saw the words on the aunty's lips and her face. She lifted her chin. She turned to her friends and signed a joke about the aunty's giant earrings, and they all burst out laughing.
Her brother Anirban came over. He'd been learning to sign since she went to the new school. He signed to her, slowly, "You okay?"
She signed back, "More than okay. I have a whole language. She has earrings."
Anirban laughed and turned to the aunty. "She talks properly, Kaki. In her language. You'd just have to learn it."

qa.q: What festival was being celebrated in the village?
qa.a: The Pola festival.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's lifted chin suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggested she felt proud and defiant, refusing to be pitied for signing.

qa.q: How did Anirban support his sister?
qa.a: He had learned to sign, checked on her in her language, and told the aunty that signing is talking properly.

qa.q: How might the aunty see signing compared with Lavanya?
qa.a: The aunty seems to see it as a sad lack, while Lavanya sees it as a complete language and a source of pride.

grounding: The scene shows a Deaf teenager's pride in signing and community, and her family treating sign language as a valid, complete language.

passage:
At the youth club in north London, Bilal and Abebe were on the same football team, and the coach was trying to organise the drills.
Bilal was Deaf and signed British Sign Language with his friends, fast and full of expression. Abebe was hard of hearing, wore hearing aids, spoke English, and knew only a little sign.
A new volunteer kept telling Abebe, "You should sign more, it's your community." Then he told Bilal, "You should practise speaking more, it'll help you get on."
Both of them looked at each other and rolled their eyes.
At the water break, Abebe said, "I like speaking. Some sign. That's me."
Bilal signed and Abebe translated: "I'm proud of signing. It's my language. That's me."
The coach, who knew them both, told the volunteer, "Let them choose."
Later Bilal taught Abebe the sign for offside, and Abebe taught Bilal a terrible joke in English.

qa.q: Where was the youth club?
qa.a: In north London.

qa.q: What did the eye-roll between Bilal and Abebe suggest?
qa.a: It suggested they both felt annoyed and patronised at being told how they should communicate.

qa.q: What did the coach get right?
qa.a: The coach told the volunteer to let each of them choose, respecting that language choice is personal.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have seen his own advice?
qa.a: He probably thought he was being helpful, not realising he was pushing his own ideas onto choices that belonged to Bilal and Abebe.

grounding: The scene shows two teenagers with different hearing and language choices, both valid, and pride in signing as a complete language.

passage:
In their village school near Margao, Maria was writing an essay for the district competition: "Should the old Friday market be moved to the new highway site?" She thought it should stay, and she was angry about it.
Her first draft said, "Only stupid people with no heart would move a market that has existed for a hundred years."
Vijay Sir read it in the staff room and tapped the line. "How would a councillor who wants to move it feel reading this?"
"Insulted," Maria admitted.
"And would they keep reading?"
"No."
So she rewrote it. Thesis first: the market should stay because it supports small farmers and is reachable on foot. Then evidence: the fish sellers who can't afford transport. Then the other side: "The highway site is cleaner and has parking, which matters." Then why she still disagreed.
Vijay Sir smiled. "Now it sounds strong, not angry."

qa.q: Where was the new site for the market?
qa.a: The new highway site.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she wrote the first draft?
qa.a: Maria felt angry and protective about the old market, and the insulting line showed it.

qa.q: What did Vijay Sir's question help Maria understand?
qa.a: That on paper, without a face or voice, word choice carries the tone, so insulting words would make readers stop listening.

qa.q: How might a councillor who favours the highway site read the final essay?
qa.a: They would likely keep reading, because it acknowledges the parking and cleanliness before explaining the other view respectfully.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager writing an essay with thesis, evidence and counterargument, and learning that tone in writing depends on word choice.

In a Singapore flat, Dalia pushed her laptop towards her friend Xin. "Read my essay on school start times. Tell me if it's convincing."
Xin read for a minute. "It's... loud."
"Loud?"
"You wrote 'obviously' five times. And 'anyone with a brain knows.' And three exclamation marks in one paragraph."
"But I'm right."
"Maybe. But it reads like you're shouting at the principal. I can't see your face. I can only see your words."
Dalia flopped back on the sofa. "Ugh. Fine."
She cut every "obviously." She added a line: "Some parents worry later starts would clash with work hours; this is a real concern." Then she answered it with the survey from her class.
Xin read the new version. "Now I'd actually agree with you."
Dalia grinned. "Obviously."

qa.q: How many times had Dalia written "obviously"?
qa.a: Dalia had written "obviously" five times.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling when Xin said the essay was loud?
qa.a: Dalia felt defensive and frustrated at first, sure of being right, then accepted the feedback.

qa.q: What changes made Dalia's essay more persuasive?
qa.a: She removed the shouting words, added the parents' concern as a counterargument, and answered it with evidence.

qa.q: How does Xin see the difference between talking and writing?
qa.a: Xin points out that a reader can't see Dalia's face, so only the words carry the tone.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager revising a persuasive essay so word choice, not face or voice, carries a respectful tone and adds a counterargument.

The school library was nearly empty after the last bell. Yamini had three pages on why the town needed more public libraries, and the essay competition closed on Friday.
Mr Darshan, the librarian, read it slowly. "Lots of good facts. What's your main point, in one sentence?"
Yamini opened her mouth. Closed it. "Libraries are... good?"
"That's a topic, not a thesis."
She tried again. "The town needs two more libraries, because students without internet at home have nowhere to study."
"That's a thesis. Now, what would someone who disagrees say?"
"That everything's online now."
"Put that in. Then show why it's not true for everyone."
Yamini wrote the thesis at the top in capital letters, crossed out half a page that didn't support it, and added a paragraph on the counterargument.
On Friday she submitted a version with half the words and twice the force.

qa.q: When did the essay competition close?
qa.a: The competition closed on Friday.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she couldn't say her main point?
qa.a: Yamini felt flustered and unsure, realising the essay had lots of facts but no clear argument.

qa.q: What made Mr Darshan's questions useful?
qa.a: They pushed Yamini to write one clear thesis and to include and answer the opposing view.

qa.q: What would change if Yamini had submitted the first draft?
qa.a: Readers might have found good facts but no clear argument, so the essay would have been less persuasive.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager building an essay around a thesis, evidence and counterargument with a librarian's guidance.

Dear Papa,
I found my diary moved on the shelf yesterday. I know you read it. I'm not shouting. I'm writing because I can say it better on paper.
That diary is where I sort myself out. When I wrote "I hate this family" last week, it was after the fight about my phone. I didn't mean I'd do anything. I was angry, I wrote it, and then I felt better and came down for dinner. Writing it is how I don't say it.
If you read it, I'll stop writing honestly, and then I'll have nowhere to put things.
I promise you this: if I'm ever worried about my safety, or someone else's, I won't keep it in a diary. I'll come to you or Mamma straight away.
Please let the diary be mine.
Sarika

qa.a: Sarika wrote "I hate this family."

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling on finding the diary moved?
qa.a: Sarika felt hurt and exposed that the private diary had been read, but tried to stay calm and explain.

qa.q: What makes Sarika's letter a good way to ask for privacy?
qa.a: It is calm, explains that writing angry words is not acting on them, and offers a clear promise to share any safety worry.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt reading "I hate this family"?
qa.a: Papa probably felt shocked and worried, which may be why he kept reading, not realising it was a way to let off steam.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager using a diary to sort feelings, asking for privacy, and promising to share safety worries with a trusted adult.

Aadhya, you asked how I, Lavanya, stay so calm. Honestly? A notebook.
Every night I write whatever's in my head. Mean things about my teachers. Crushes. Whether I'm pretty. Stuff I'd never say. Some nights I write "I'm quitting school" and in the morning I laugh and go.
Writing something down isn't a plan. It's just a place to put it.
But there was one time it was different. For a week I wrote about a man near my tuition who kept walking behind me and asking my name. I wrote it three nights in a row. On the fourth night I read those pages back and thought, this isn't a feeling. This is a safety thing.
So I went and woke my mother right then. She listened, told me I did the right thing, and the next morning she walked me to tuition and spoke to the tuition owner.
The notebook is private. But not for that.

qa.q: How many nights did Lavanya write about the man near tuition?
qa.a: Lavanya wrote it three nights in a row.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on the fourth night?
qa.a: Lavanya felt worried and alarmed, realising the pages described a real safety concern, not just a passing feeling.

qa.q: Which choice of Lavanya's worked, and why?
qa.a: Going to wake the mother that night worked, because it turned a private worry into action, and the mother acted the next morning.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother have felt being woken with this?
qa.a: She was probably worried but relieved that Lavanya told her, and she responded calmly and protectively.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager using a private journal to sort feelings, and knowing that safety worries must be shared with a trusted adult.

I'm Jaya, Arnab's sister, three years older. This summer Arnab started carrying a small black notebook everywhere. He'd write on the terrace, at the dinner table, on the bus.
One afternoon he left it on the sofa. I'll be honest: I picked it up. I wanted to know if he was okay, because he'd been quieter since the fight with his best friend.
I held it for a whole minute. Then I put it down without opening it.
That evening I said, "You left your notebook out. I didn't read it."
He looked at me hard, then relaxed. "Thanks."
"If anything in there ever scares you, or you're worried about someone's safety, you'll tell me or Amma, right?"
"Yeah. It's mostly just me being annoyed."
A week later he read me one line he'd written about his friend. He chose it. That felt better than anything I could have read.

qa.a: It was a small black notebook.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling while holding the notebook for a whole minute?
qa.a: Jaya felt worried about Arnab after the fight with his friend and tempted to read, but torn, because it would break his trust.

qa.q: What did Jaya get right?
qa.a: She respected his privacy, told him honestly, and made sure he knew to share any safety worry with her or Amma.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt if Jaya had read the notebook?
qa.a: He would probably have felt betrayed and might have stopped writing honestly or trusting her.

grounding: A sister's account shows respect for a teenager's private journal, with the understanding that safety worries should be shared.
